name: Bhavatarini Shmashanpith Kali Temple
significance: A Kali temple raised in 1994 on a plot that had served the village of Balidangri as a Hindu cremation ground. Night worship kept up there for decades by local residents was eventually formalised into a permanent shrine to Bhavatarini, a form of Kali.

name: Iswara Temple, Jalasangvi
significance: An eleventh-century Shiva temple attributed to the reign of Vikramaditya VI, with a dance hall on eight pillars, a Nandi chamber and a linga sanctum. Its salabhanjika bracket figures are regarded as a source for the later Hoysala bracket-figure tradition.

name: Sree Vasudevapuram Mahavishnu Temple
significance: A Vishnu temple near Aluva whose idol shows the god embracing Mahalakshmi, so that worship here is addressed jointly to Vishnu and to Lakshmi in her eight forms. After a long decline under its early Brahmin custodians the temple's standing was restored through the intervention of Vilwamangalam Swamikal, and the Tambula Samarpanam offering remains its central rite.
story: Mahalakshmi is said to have promised to appear here in eight forms over the eight days beginning at Akshaya Tritiya, granting a different boon in each.

name: Virundeeswarar Temple
significance: One of the older Shiva temples of the Coimbatore region, credited to Chola kings and reckoned over 1,300 years old, with a self-manifested linga and a second linga in the sanctum. It is administered by the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department.
story: Sundaramurthy Nayanar is said to have been fed here by an old couple who then revealed themselves as Shiva and Parvati; because the god offered virundhu, a feast, he is called Virundeeswarar.

name: Kanadikavu Shree Vishnumaya Kuttichathan Swamy Temple
significance: Described as the oldest temple in Kerala dedicated to Vishnumaya Kuttichathan, some 20 km from Thrissur, where 390 Kuttichathans are venerated as attendant deities alongside shrines to Bhadrakali, Bhuvaneswari, Nagaraja and Brahmarakshas.
story: A sage remembered as Koonamuthappan is said to have won mantras from the Goddess through severe penance, meditated in the Himalayas, and returned to Peringottukara to install Chathan Swamy for the good of humankind.

name: Kankaleshwar Temple
significance: A star-plan Shiva temple at Beed, its domed roof carried on twenty-four pillars and its niches filled with carved gods and goddesses. No inscription records its date; after the region passed to a Muslim kingdom a parapet was added on the roof for prayers there while Hindu worship continued below, and it was then known as the Khanqah Deval.

name: Idangazhi Nayanar Temple, Kodumbalur
significance: A Shiva temple at Kodumbalur commemorating Idangazhi Nayanar, the local king counted among the Saiva saints, who built temples and endowed worship in the town. Aippasi Karthigai is among the festivals kept here.
story: A devotee who had spent everything on worship stole paddy from the royal store; on hearing why, Idangazhi freed him and threw the granary open to all who needed grain for offerings to Shiva.

name: Chengalamma Parameshwari Temple
builtDisplay: 10th c. (Chola shrine); worship from the 4th–5th c.
significance: A goddess temple on the bank of the Kalangi river at the southern edge of Sullurpeta, whose worship is traced to the fourth and fifth centuries and whose first built shrine, a small hut, is credited to the Cholas around the tenth century. The image is revered as Trikale Chengali, its left side read as Parvati, its right as Saraswati and its centre as Mahalakshmi.

name: Agastheesvarar Temple, Purisai
significance: A Shiva temple at Purisai whose presiding deity is Agastheesvarar and whose goddess is Akilandesvari. It is counted among the Vaippu Sthalams, shrines named in passing in the hymns of the Nayanar Sundarar.

name: Tarkeshwar Nath Temple
builtDisplay: c. 1727, with the founding of Jaipur
significance: One of the best known of the old Shiva temples that earned Jaipur the name Chhoti Kashi, dated to about 1727 and believed to have been laid out by the city's planner Vidyadhar Bhattacharya. Its priesthood was entrusted to Vyas family priests brought from Amer, and Mahashivaratri and the Mondays of Shravan draw the largest crowds.
story: After a fight between a lion and a goat on the spot, a voice is said to have risen from the ground; digging there uncovered the self-manifested Shivalinga now worshipped in the temple.

name: Trinetreshwar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Tarnetar attributed to the Pratihara ruler Mihira Bhoja in the eighth century. It is best known today for the Trinetreshwar Mahadev Mela, the annual fair held around it.

name: Devunigutta Temple
significance: A sixth-century Shiva temple on a forested plateau some 60 km east of Warangal, its carving dominated by Ardhanarishvara and close in feeling to Gupta-period sculpture. Recorded by the Archaeological Survey of India in 2012 but left abandoned, it drew wide attention only when photographs of it spread online in 2017.

name: Rudrakodisvarar Temple, Tirukalukundram
significance: A Shiva temple at Tirukalukundram whose presiding deity is Rudrakodisvarar and whose goddess is Tiripurasundari, the main shrine facing east and hers facing south. It is counted among the Vaippu Sthalams named in the hymns of the Nayanar Appar.

name: Nameswara Temple, Pillalamarri
dynasty: Recherla Reddi, feudatories of the Kakatiyas
significance: A Saiva temple on the bank of the Musi built about 1202 by Namireddi of the Recherla Reddi family, vassals of the Kakatiyas, and named for him. It is one of four closely carved stone and granite temples of the Kakatiya era at Pillalamarri, its pillars finely worked but heavily defaced.

name: Erakeswara Temple, Pillalamarri
dynasty: Recherla Reddi, feudatories of the Kakatiyas
significance: A Saiva temple at Pillalamarri commissioned in the early thirteenth century by Erakasani, wife of the Recherla chief Beti Reddi, and named lord of Eraka after her. Its workmanship is close to that of the Ramappa temple and Kota Gullu; vandalised during the raids of Alauddin Khilji, it was re-established by 1357 under a chief serving Kapaya Nayaka of the Musunuri line.

name: Tungareshwar Temple
significance: A Shiva temple on the Tungareshwar plateau above Vasai, more than 2,000 feet up, with a shrine to the goddess Khodiyar Mata beside it and a linga ringed by a brass serpent. Mahashivaratri and the Mondays of Shravan bring the largest gatherings and a communal feast.
story: Parashurama is said to have killed a demon named Tunga at this spot, and the temple to have been raised in his honour.

name: Pazhavangadi Ganapathy Temple
significance: A Ganesha temple at East Fort, close to the Padmanabhaswamy temple, whose seated image was kept by the Nair Brigade at Padmanabhapuram and installed here when the brigade moved to Thiruvananthapuram. It passed to the Indian Army after the state forces were integrated, and holds thirty-two further sculptures of Ganesha.

name: Mudhai Devi Temple
deity: Mudhai Devi (with an Uma-Maheshwara image in the sanctum)
significance: A partly ruined twelfth-century goddess temple in the Khandesh village of Waghali, built on a stellate plan with twenty-four pillars carrying sanctum, ardhamandapa, mandapa and portico. The Archaeological Survey of India declared it a monument of national importance in 1914.

name: Mahadev Temple, Deobaloda
significance: A thirteenth-century Kalachuri Shiva temple at Deobaloda, protected by the Archaeological Survey of India, whose shikhara is now missing. Local tradition that it went up in only six months earned it the nickname the six-month temple, and a stepped tank beside it is held to be linked to Arang by a tunnel.
story: The sculptor is said to have worked so absorbed that he laboured naked; when his sister came with his food both leapt into the ponds in shame, and he is said to have taken the tunnel from the tank to Arang, where he turned to stone.

name: Dronacharya Temple, Gurugram
significance: A temple to Dronacharya, the teacher of the Pandavas and Kauravas after whom Gurugram is named, founded in 1872 by Singha Bharat, a devotee of Drona's wife Shitala Devi. It grew from a single room to two and is looked after today by five families.

name: Sri Aastik Swami Mandir, Raebareli
significance: A temple on the bank of the Sai river at Lalupur, about 10 km from Raebareli town, counted among the principal places of worship in India for Aastik Swami, revered as the lord of snakes. Nagpanchami is its main festival.
story: In the Mahabharata account retold here, Astika halted Janamejaya's snake sacrifice and saved the serpents, who in return blessed him so that those who worship him are protected from venomous creatures.

name: Nilkanth Temple, Mandu
significance: A Shiva temple at Mandu raised over an older shrine between April 1574 and April 1575 by Shah Badgah, Akbar's governor of Mandu, and commissioned by the emperor for his Hindu consort Mariam-uz-Zamani. Built to serve as both palace and temple, it is now used purely as a temple and draws pilgrims from across India.
story: The name Neelkanth, the blue-throated one, is traced to Shiva swallowing the Halahala poison churned from the ocean, which stained his throat blue.

name: Gadarmal Devi Temple
significance: A sandstone yogini temple at Badoh with a rectangular shrine under a tall massive shikhara, forty-two niches for goddess images and seven subsidiary shrines around it; eighteen of the broken goddess figures that once sat in its grooves survive. It is compared with the Teli ka Mandir at Gwalior and now holds both Hindu and Jain images.
story: Locals hold that the temple was raised by shepherds, gadariya, which is how it came by the name Gadarmal.

name: Keezhtali Mahadeva Temple
significance: A Shiva temple at Kodungallur counted among the 108 Shiva temples of the Chera country and one of its four thali temples, which held a place in the administration of ancient Kerala. It is among the few Hindu temples recorded as destroyed during Tipu Sultan's campaign.
story: Folklore holds that the sage Parashurama himself installed the Shiva image here.

name: Na-Pukhuri Shiva Dol
significance: A 26 m Shiva temple on the south bank of the Rudrasagar tank, some 8 km from Sivasagar, built in 1773 in the reign of Lakshmi Singha under the supervision of Madan Darika Hajarika and consecrated under Gaurinath Singha. It is the last temple of the Ahom period and marks the end of that kingdom's temple building.

name: Jwala Ji Temple, Khrew
significance: A twentieth-century shrine at Khrew commissioned by Raja Daya Krishna Kaul to Jwala Ji, the family goddess of many Kashmiri Hindu households. Kalhana's Rajatarangini names the village as Khaduvi and describes its springs; the annual Jwalamukhi fair here is kept by Hindus and Muslims alike.
story: The goddess is said to have shown herself first as a radiant flame, and to have settled here for good after stopping the gods on their way to seize Kubera's treasure.

name: Sanchareswar Mahadev Temple
significance: A Shiva temple in the village of Umarda in Udaipur district, worshipped as Sanchareswar Mahadev. The published account of it is slight and records neither a date nor a patron.

name: Altharakkal Sree Muthappan Madapura
significance: A madapura, or shrine, to Muthappan in Pullur village about 6 km from Kanhangad in northern Kerala, built in the kavu idiom of the region. Local tradition treats Muthappan as a manifestation of Shiva.
